questions.question: A 26-year-old woman comes to a sexual health clinic for routine screening. She has a new male partner, no genitourinary symptoms, and a normal pelvic examination. The clinic is piloting a rapid point-of-care urine test for Chlamydia trachomatis, which was validated in 500 women against nucleic acid amplification testing (reference standard). The validation results are shown. Her rapid test is negative. Based on these data, which of the following is the probability that she truly does not have chlamydial infection?

explanations.A: 75% is the sensitivity (90/120), the proportion of infected women who test positive; it does not describe a patient with a negative result.
explanations.B: 78% is simply the fraction of all women who tested negative (390/500), not the fraction of negatives who are truly uninfected.
explanations.C: 82% is the positive predictive value (90/110), which applies to a patient with a positive result.
explanations.D: Correct. The negative predictive value is true negatives divided by all negative tests: 360/(360 + 30) = 360/390 = 92%.
explanations.E: 95% is the specificity (360/380), the proportion of uninfected women who test negative; it starts from disease status rather than from the test result.

questions.question: A blood test for preeclampsia with a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 95% was validated at a tertiary referral center, where 30% of tested women had preeclampsia. A 29-year-old primigravid woman at 24 weeks' gestation is seen at a community clinic. Her blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and urinalysis shows no protein. The clinic offers the test to all its pregnant patients, among whom the prevalence of preeclampsia is about 2%. Compared with the referral-center population, which of the following values of the test will be substantially lower in the community-clinic population?

explanations.A: Negative predictive value rises, not falls, as prevalence decreases, because nearly everyone who tests negative is truly disease-free.
explanations.B: The positive likelihood ratio (0.90/0.05 = 18) is built only from sensitivity and specificity, so it does not vary with disease prevalence.
explanations.C: Correct. Predictive values depend on prevalence; at 30% prevalence the PPV is about 89%, but at 2% it falls to about 27% because false positives from the many healthy women outnumber true positives.
explanations.D: Sensitivity is a characteristic of the test, measured only among women who have the disease, so it does not change with prevalence.
explanations.E: Specificity is a characteristic of the test, measured only among women without the disease, so it does not change with prevalence.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of irregular menses and increasing facial hair over the past 2 years. Her BMI is 31 kg/m² and there is coarse hair on the upper lip and chin. The physician reviews a study of a new ultrasound criterion for polycystic ovary syndrome, which reports a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 90%. Which of the following is the positive likelihood ratio of this criterion?

explanations.A: 0.22 is the negative likelihood ratio, (1 - 0.80)/0.90, which applies to a negative result.
explanations.B: 0.80 is the sensitivity itself; the LR+ must also account for how often the test is positive in women without the disease.
explanations.C: 4.0 is sensitivity divided by (1 - sensitivity), which wrongly uses diseased patients in both numerator and denominator.
explanations.D: Correct. LR+ = sensitivity/(1 - specificity) = 0.80/0.10 = 8.0, the probability of a positive result in diseased persons divided by that in nondiseased persons.
explanations.E: 9.0 is specificity divided by (1 - specificity), which uses only nondiseased persons and ignores sensitivity.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 3 weeks after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery because of 2 days of mild left calf discomfort. The calves are equal in circumference and there is no erythema. Based on her history and examination, the physician estimates her pretest probability of deep venous thrombosis at 20%. A D-dimer assay with the characteristics shown is ordered and the result is negative. Which of the following is closest to her posttest probability of deep venous thrombosis?

explanations.A: 2.0% comes from multiplying the pretest probability (0.20) directly by the LR-; likelihood ratios must be applied to odds, not probabilities.
explanations.C: 9.1% converts the LR- itself to a probability (0.1/1.1) and ignores the pretest odds entirely.
explanations.D: 10% treats the LR- of 0.1 as if it were a probability of disease.
explanations.E: 20% is the unchanged pretest probability, which would be correct only if the likelihood ratio were 1.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of 3 days of mild lower abdominal pain. She is sexually active with one partner and uses condoms inconsistently. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F). There is no cervical motion tenderness. The physician estimates a 10% pretest probability of pelvic inflammatory disease and orders a test with a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 90%. The result is positive. Which of the following is her posttest probability of pelvic inflammatory disease?

explanations.A: 1% results from dividing by the LR+ instead of multiplying, which would mean a positive result lowered the probability.
explanations.B: 10% is the unchanged pretest probability; a positive result with an LR+ above 1 must raise the odds of disease.
explanations.C: 47% comes from using the pretest probability (0.1) as if it were odds: 0.1 × 9 = 0.9, then 0.9/1.9; the probability must first be converted to odds.
explanations.D: Correct. LR+ = 0.90/(1 - 0.90) = 9; pretest odds = 0.1/0.9 = 1/9; posttest odds = 1/9 × 9 = 1; probability = 1/(1 + 1) = 50%.
explanations.E: 90% comes from multiplying the pretest probability by the LR+ (0.1 × 9), or from equating the sensitivity with the chance of disease after a positive test.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of oligomenorrhea and acne for 1 year. Her BMI is 27 kg/m². The physician orders a newly marketed serum marker for polycystic ovary syndrome; the manufacturer reports a sensitivity of 60% and a specificity of 40%. Her result is positive. Which of the following best describes the effect of this positive result on her likelihood of polycystic ovary syndrome?

answers.C: Leaves the probability of disease unchanged
answers.D: Raises the probability of disease by 60%

explanations.A: Only a likelihood ratio below 1 lowers the odds of disease; here the LR+ is exactly 1.
explanations.B: Doubling the odds would require an LR+ of 2; here LR+ = 0.60/(1 - 0.40) = 1.
explanations.C: Correct. LR+ = 0.60/0.60 = 1, meaning the result is equally likely in women with and without the disease, so posttest odds equal pretest odds.
explanations.D: Sensitivity is not an amount by which probability rises; the change depends on the likelihood ratio, which is 1 here.
explanations.E: A test that is positive as often in healthy women as in affected women cannot rule in disease; that requires a large LR+.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of right lower quadrant pain and nausea for 12 hours. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test is negative. The physician estimates a 10% pretest probability of a particular diagnosis and orders a test whose positive likelihood ratio is 20. The result is positive. Using the nomogram shown, which of the following best approximates her posttest probability?

image.caption: Fagan nomogram
image.credit: Notes p. 5 (Nicoll et al., Guide to Diagnostic Tests, 7th ed., McGraw-Hill)

explanations.A: 20% is the value of the likelihood ratio, not a probability; the line must be continued to the posttest probability axis.
explanations.B: 30% would correspond to an LR+ of about 4 from a 10% pretest probability.
explanations.C: 50% would correspond to an LR+ of about 9 from a 10% pretest probability.
explanations.D: Correct. A straight line from 10% on the pretest axis through 20 on the LR axis reaches about 70% on the posttest axis (by calculation, odds 1/9 × 20 = 2.2, probability 69%).
explanations.E: 90% would require an LR+ of about 80 from a 10% pretest probability.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. Her blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg and she has mild ankle edema. Her physician wants a blood test that, if negative, will most strongly lower the probability of preeclampsia. Five assays have been evaluated, with the characteristics shown. Which assay, if negative, will produce the greatest decrease in the odds of preeclampsia?

explanations.A: Assay V has the highest sensitivity, but its poor specificity gives an LR- of 0.01/0.30 = 0.033, so a negative result is less powerful than with assay Z.
explanations.B: Assay W has an excellent specificity but an LR- of 0.15/0.99 = 0.15, so a negative result lowers the odds only modestly.
explanations.C: Assay X has an LR- of 0.05/0.80 = 0.063, weaker than assay Z.
explanations.D: Assay Y has the lowest sensitivity and an LR- of 0.25/0.95 = 0.26, the least useful for ruling out.
explanations.E: Correct. Assay Z has the lowest LR- = (1 - 0.98)/0.95 = 0.021; the diagnostic power of a negative result depends on both sensitivity and specificity, not sensitivity alone.

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of sudden, severe left lower quadrant pain and vomiting for 3 hours. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Pulse is 104/min and the left adnexa is tender. The physician considers five bedside findings for ovarian torsion, with the characteristics shown. Which finding, if present, would most increase the probability of ovarian torsion?

explanations.A: Finding P has a high sensitivity but an LR+ of 0.98/0.30 = 3.3, so its presence raises the odds only slightly.
explanations.B: Finding Q has the highest specificity, but its low sensitivity gives an LR+ of 0.20/0.01 = 20, less than finding T; SpPin alone is misleading.
explanations.C: Finding R has an LR+ of 0.80/0.10 = 8.
explanations.D: Finding S has an LR+ of 0.95/0.15 = 6.3.
explanations.E: Correct. Finding T has the largest LR+ = 0.90/(1 - 0.98) = 45, so a positive finding multiplies the pretest odds the most.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman is evaluated in the emergency department for lower abdominal pain and vaginal discharge for 4 days. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). Based on history and examination, her pretest probability of pelvic inflammatory disease is estimated at 50%. Her leukocyte count is normal (a negative result), but pelvic ultrasonography shows findings consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease (a positive result). The likelihood ratios for these results are shown. Which of the following is her posttest probability of pelvic inflammatory disease?

explanations.A: 33% applies only the negative leukocyte count (odds 1 × 0.5 = 0.5) and ignores the positive ultrasound.
explanations.B: 50% assumes the two results cancel; they are not equal and opposite, because 0.5 × 4 = 2, not 1.
explanations.C: Correct. Pretest odds = 0.5/0.5 = 1; posttest odds = 1 × 0.5 × 4 = 2; probability = 2/(2 + 1) = 67%. Multiple LRs are applied in series by multiplying them all into the pretest odds.
explanations.D: 80% applies only the positive ultrasound (odds 1 × 4 = 4) and ignores the normal leukocyte count.
explanations.E: 89% comes from dividing by the LR- (1/0.5 × 4 = 8) instead of multiplying, which wrongly treats the negative result as raising the odds.

questions.question: A 21-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 2 days of vaginal spotting and lower abdominal discomfort. A home urine pregnancy test was positive and her last menstrual period was about 5 weeks ago. She has no risk factors for ectopic pregnancy. Vital signs and physical examination are normal. Her pretest probability of ectopic pregnancy is estimated at 15%. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows neither an intrauterine nor an ectopic pregnancy. Serum β-hCG is 1748 mIU/mL. The characteristics of transvaginal ultrasonography are shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.D: Repeat urine pregnancy test in 1 week

explanations.A: Laparoscopy is for a positive ultrasound, which raises even a low-risk patient's probability too high not to explore; her ultrasound is negative.
explanations.B: Her posttest probability is about 2.1% (odds 0.176 × 0.12 = 0.021), still above the 2% threshold most emergency physicians accept for ruling out a life-threatening illness.
explanations.C: Methotrexate treats a diagnosed ectopic pregnancy; a negative ultrasound has lowered her probability to about 2%, so there is no diagnosis to treat.
explanations.D: A urine pregnancy test is already known to be positive and is not quantitative, so repeating it gives no trend and no additional likelihood ratio.
explanations.E: Correct. A negative ultrasound lowers her probability to about 2.1%, not low enough; serial β-hCGs every 48-72 hours confirm a downward trend, and each declining value carries an LR- that pushes the probability lower.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of mild vaginal spotting for 1 day. A urine pregnancy test is positive. She has no pain, no risk factors for ectopic pregnancy, and normal vital signs and examination; her pretest probability of ectopic pregnancy is estimated at 2%. Transvaginal ultrasonography, which has a positive likelihood ratio of 111 for ectopic pregnancy, shows an extrauterine gestational sac in the right adnexa. Which of the following is closest to her posttest probability of ectopic pregnancy?

explanations.A: 2% is the unchanged pretest probability; a positive result with an LR+ of 111 greatly increases the odds.
explanations.B: 18% would correspond to an LR+ of only about 11 from a 2% pretest probability.
explanations.C: 41% would correspond to an LR+ of about 34 from a 2% pretest probability.
explanations.D: Correct. Pretest odds = 0.02/0.98 = 0.0204; posttest odds = 0.0204 × 111 = 2.27; probability = 2.27/3.27 = 69%, high enough that such a patient goes to the OR for exploration.
explanations.E: 95% is the posttest probability for a patient with a 15% pretest probability (odds 0.176 × 111 = 19.5); a lower starting probability gives a lower result.

questions.question: A state health department pilots a serum screening assay in newborns for a rare inherited endocrine disorder with a prevalence of 1 per 1,000 births. The assay has a sensitivity of 100% and a specificity of 95%. A 3-day-old boy born at term with normal growth and no ambiguous features has a positive screen; his parents are told that most positive screens in the program are false positives. Which of the following changes in the assay would most increase its positive predictive value in this population?

answers.A: Higher sensitivity at the same specificity
answers.B: Higher specificity at the same sensitivity
answers.D: Lower cutoff for a positive result

explanations.A: Sensitivity is already 100%; true positives cannot increase, and the problem is the number of false positives.
explanations.B: Correct. When a disease is infrequent, PPV depends heavily on specificity; at 95% specificity about 50 of every 1,000 healthy newborns test positive versus 1 true case (PPV about 2%), so fewer false positives raise PPV most.
explanations.C: A larger study narrows confidence intervals but does not change the true sensitivity, specificity, or prevalence that determine PPV.
explanations.D: Lowering the cutoff makes the test more sensitive and less specific, adding false positives and lowering PPV.
explanations.E: Retesting negatives targets false negatives, which do not exist at 100% sensitivity and do not affect PPV.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 26 weeks' gestation has a BMI of 33 kg/m² and a history of gestational diabetes mellitus in her first pregnancy. Her physician estimates a 25% probability of gestational diabetes in this pregnancy and plans to apply the likelihood ratio of a screening test result. Before the likelihood ratio can be applied, which of the following is her pretest odds of gestational diabetes?

explanations.A: 0.25 is the pretest probability itself; likelihood ratios must be multiplied by odds, so the probability must first be converted.
explanations.C: 0.75 is 1 - p, the probability that she does not have gestational diabetes.
explanations.D: 1.33 is 1/(1 - p), which is not a measure of odds.
explanations.E: 3.0 is the odds against disease, (1 - p)/p, the inverse of the correct value.

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 18 hours of periumbilical pain that has moved to the right lower quadrant. A urine pregnancy test is negative. She has right lower quadrant tenderness without rebound. The physician estimates a 25% pretest probability of appendicitis. Her leukocyte count is 13,000/mm³. Interval likelihood ratios for the leukocyte count are shown. Which of the following is closest to her posttest probability of appendicitis?

explanations.A: 10% uses the LR of 0.34 from the 10 to <12 row; her count of 13,000/mm³ falls in the 12 to <15 interval.
explanations.B: 25% is the unchanged pretest probability; her result carries an LR of 2.70, not 1.
explanations.C: Correct. Pretest odds = 0.25/0.75 = 1/3; posttest odds = 1/3 × 2.70 = 0.90; probability = 0.90/1.90 = 47%. Interval LRs let the LR change with the value of the result.
explanations.D: 68% comes from multiplying the pretest probability by the LR (0.25 × 2.70); LRs apply to odds.
explanations.E: 73% converts the LR of 2.70 directly to a probability (2.70/3.70) and ignores the pretest odds.

questions.question: A 33-year-old physician who trained at a tertiary referral center joins a rural women's health clinic, where most diseases she tests for are far less common. A 40-year-old woman with fatigue and weight gain asks how likely she is to have a thyroid disorder if her screening test is abnormal. The physician wants a test characteristic that does not vary with disease prevalence but, combined with this patient's own pretest probability, gives the probability of disease after a particular result. Which of the following test characteristics best meets both requirements?

explanations.A: Correct. Likelihood ratios are numerically stable across prevalence like sensitivity and specificity, yet, like predictive values, they tell how likely disease is given a particular result once applied to pretest odds.
explanations.B: NPV answers the clinical question for a negative result but varies with prevalence, so the referral-center value would not transfer to the rural clinic.
explanations.C: PPV answers the clinical question for a positive result but falls as prevalence falls, so it cannot be carried over between populations.
explanations.D: Sensitivity is stable across prevalence but assumes disease status is already known; it does not by itself give the probability of disease after a result.
explanations.E: Specificity is stable across prevalence but describes only people without disease; it does not by itself give the probability of disease after a result.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of irregular menses and hirsutism. A new serum test for polycystic ovary syndrome was evaluated in a study with the results shown. Among women referred to this clinic with similar complaints, 40% have polycystic ovary syndrome. Her test result is positive. Which of the following is the probability that she has polycystic ovary syndrome?

explanations.A: 10% is the false positive rate (30/300), the proportion of women without the disease who test positive.
explanations.B: 40% is her pretest probability, which a positive test with an LR+ of 9 must raise.
explanations.C: Correct. Sensitivity = 180/200 = 90% and specificity = 270/300 = 90%, so LR+ = 9; pretest odds = 0.4/0.6 = 0.67; posttest odds = 6; probability = 6/7 = 86% (the PPV at 40% prevalence).
explanations.D: 90% is the sensitivity, the proportion of affected women who test positive, which starts from disease status rather than from her result.
explanations.E: 93% is the negative predictive value at this prevalence, which applies to a woman with a negative result.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of oligomenorrhea and acne. A medical student reads that the serum test the physician has ordered has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 92%. The result returns positive, and the student wants to calculate the probability that this patient has polycystic ovary syndrome. In addition to the test's sensitivity, specificity, and result, which of the following is required for this calculation?

answers.A: Clinic prevalence of polycystic ovary syndrome
answers.C: Number of patients in the validation study
answers.D: Positive predictive value from the original study

explanations.A: Correct. Bayesian logic needs three things to reach a posttest probability: the prevalence of disease in the population being evaluated (her pretest probability), the test's sensitivity and specificity, and the test result.
explanations.B: A confidence interval describes the precision of the sensitivity estimate but does not supply a starting probability for this patient.
explanations.C: Study size affects precision, not the patient's starting probability, which is the missing piece.
explanations.D: The PPV from the original study reflects that study's prevalence and does not transfer to a population with a different prevalence.
explanations.E: Cost bears on whether to test, not on calculating the probability of disease after the result.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of vaginal spotting and mild pelvic pain for 1 day. A urine pregnancy test is positive. Vital signs are normal. Based on history, her pretest probability of ectopic pregnancy is estimated at 15%. Bimanual examination elicits cervical motion tenderness, which has a positive likelihood ratio of 4.9 for ectopic pregnancy. Which of the following is closest to her probability of ectopic pregnancy after this finding?

explanations.A: 15% is the unchanged pretest probability; a finding with an LR+ of 4.9 raises the odds.
explanations.B: Correct. Pretest odds = 0.15/0.85 = 0.176; posttest odds = 0.176 × 4.9 = 0.86; probability = 0.86/1.86 = 46%, so this exam finding alone neither rules ectopic pregnancy in nor out.
explanations.C: 74% comes from multiplying the pretest probability by the LR+ (0.15 × 4.9); LRs apply to odds, not probabilities.
explanations.D: 83% converts the LR+ directly to a probability (4.9/5.9) and ignores the pretest odds.
explanations.E: 95% is the posttest probability after a positive transvaginal ultrasound (LR+ 111), not after cervical motion tenderness.

questions.question: A clinic introduces a hypothetical two-step screening program for gestational diabetes. All pregnant women receive test 1 (sensitivity 90%, specificity 80%); only those who test positive go on to test 2 (sensitivity 80%, specificity 95%), and a woman is diagnosed only if both tests are positive. A 30-year-old woman at 25 weeks' gestation with a BMI of 30 kg/m² and a family history of type 2 diabetes enters the program. Which of the following is the net sensitivity of this two-step program?

explanations.A: Correct. In sequential testing, a woman with the disease must test positive on both tests, so net sensitivity = 0.90 × 0.80 = 72%; sequential testing trades sensitivity for specificity (net specificity = 0.80 + 0.95 - 0.76 = 99%).
explanations.B: 80% is the sensitivity of test 2 alone, ignoring the affected women already missed by test 1.
explanations.C: 85% averages the two sensitivities, which has no meaning for combined testing.
explanations.D: 90% is the sensitivity of test 1 alone; requiring a second positive test can only lose additional true cases.
explanations.E: 98% is the net sensitivity of simultaneous testing (positive on either test: 0.90 + 0.80 - 0.72), not sequential testing.
